extracted.intended_audience: trial judges, patent litigators, and jurors in U.S. federal patent trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials in U.S. federal courts that define legal standards and jury decision rules on claim construction, infringement (direct and indirect), invalidity, equitable defenses, damages (lost profits and reasonable royalty), and willfulness. Designed for use by judges in charging juries and for lawyers to frame evidence and argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: The role of the claims of a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains that the claims of a patent define the invention and establish the scope of the patentee's rights; they are what the patent owner must prove the defendant infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should be instructed that the claims, not the specification or prosecution history alone, define what is covered by the patent; claims must be construed to determine their meaning and scope before applying infringement standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: How a claim defines what it covers
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must be interpreted to determine which devices, methods, or products it covers. The claim language gives notice of what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide jurors guidance on reading claim terms in context of the patent as a whole and applying court's claim construction; emphasize plain meaning unless special definitions provided in the specification or by the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes independent claims (stand-alone recitations of the invention) from dependent claims (which refer back to and further limit another claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should understand that dependent claims incorporate the limitations of the claims they depend from and may be narrower in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation / claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides the standard approach and rules for interpreting claim language, including reliance on intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) and, when appropriate, extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court's construction of disputed claim terms is binding on the jury; instruct jury to apply those constructions when determining infringement or validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112, paragraph 6 (means-plus-function) claim requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains the rules for claims that invoke 35 U.S.C. §112, para.6 (means-plus-function), i.e., when a claim recites a function to be performed rather than structure, the claim is construed to cover the corresponding structure disclosed in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim limitation is governed by §112 ¶6, the jury must compare the accused device to the claimed function and the corresponding structure (and equivalents) disclosed in the patent's specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Sets the overarching requirement that the patent owner must prove infringement of at least one claim of the patent by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct jurors that infringement analysis requires comparing accused product/method to the properly construed claim limitations; all claim limitations must be met (either literally or under doctrine of equivalents) for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — Literal infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct (literal) infringement occurs when the accused product or action meets every limitation of a claim exactly as construed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must find that each claim limitation is present in the accused product or method as previously defined by the court; if any claim limitation is missing, there is no literal infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — Literal infringement of §112, para.6 claim requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim limitation is governed by §112 ¶6, literal infringement requires that the accused product include the structure corresponding to the claimed function as disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must compare accused device to the specification's disclosed structure for the claimed function; mere performance of the function is insufficient absent the corresponding structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — Doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if the accused product or process does not literally meet the claim limitations but performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide jurors with the function-way-result test and caution them about limitations on the doctrine (e.g., prosecution history estoppel, prior art) and that it cannot be used to vitiate a claim limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on direct infringement under the doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains restrictions on applying the doctrine of equivalents, including that it cannot be applied so broadly as to cover what the patentee gave up during prosecution or to read out claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should consider prosecution history, claim amendments, and prior art when deciding whether equivalents are barred or limited; the doctrine is fact-specific and cannot erase claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — Active inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: Active inducement requires proof that the defendant knowingly induced another to infringe and possessed specific intent to encourage infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must find both that a third party directly infringed and that the defendant took affirmative steps to induce that infringement with knowledge/intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — Contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement occurs where a defendant sells a component especially made or adapted for use in a patented invention, knowing it is especially made for use in an infringement, and the component is not a staple article suitable for substantial noninfringing use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should evaluate knowledge, the nature of the component (specially made vs staple), and whether the component has substantial noninfringing uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement through supply of components from United States for combination abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses liability where defendant supplies components from the U.S. that are later combined abroad in a way that would infringe if done in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must follow statutory and case-law rules on extraterritoriality and determine whether supplying U.S. components gives rise to infringement under applicable law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by sale, offer for sale, use, or importation of a product made outside the United States by patented process
rubrics_metrics.description: Covers infringement issues when an accused product made overseas by a patented process is later sold, offered for sale, used, or imported into the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should be instructed on relevant statutory provisions and case law that govern process patents and extraterritorial activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement: one or more system components located outside the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains when a system claim may or may not be infringed if some components are located outside the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must consider whether the acts in the U.S. satisfy all claim limitations under controlling precedent (e.g., whether control/benefit theory or joint enterprise applies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement: acts of multiple parties must be combined to meet all claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses situations where no single party performs all claim steps, but collective acts of multiple parties might meet claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should be instructed on standards for attributing others' actions to the defendant (e.g., contractual arrangements, directions, control) and the limitations on proving infringement by divided performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — Elements (objective and subjective prongs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Willfulness requires proof that the defendant was aware of the patent and acted despite an objectively high likelihood that its actions infringed a valid patent, and that this objectively high likelihood was known or so obvious that it should have been known to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should consider the totality of the circumstances (including intentional copying, reliance on legal advice, and substantive defenses). The defendant's actual state of mind is not considered for the objective prong; willfulness must be proven to a high probability standard (more likely than not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — Totality of the circumstances factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists non-exhaustive factors the jury may consider in determining willfulness: intentional copying, reliance on competent legal advice, presentation of substantial defenses (including invalidity or unenforceability), and other circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct jurors that they must weigh all relevant circumstances and may consider the absence of a legal opinion as one factor but cannot assume that such an opinion would have been unfavorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — Absence of legal opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant does not claim reliance on a legal opinion to rebut willfulness, the jury may consider the lack of an opinion as a factor but may not assume the opinion would have been unfavorable; absence alone is insufficient to prove willfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may give a special instruction when lack of opinion is at issue; jurors should not treat absence of counsel's opinion as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — Burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains that a defendant asserting invalidity bears the burden of proving the patent is invalid by clear and convincing evidence (subject to governing precedents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should be instructed on which factual predicates require clear and convincing proof and where the burden lies for each asserted ground of invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity — Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent specification must contain a written description that shows the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury evaluates whether the specification reasonably conveys to a skilled artisan that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter; look for adequate disclosure of claimed features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity — Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should consider the scope of the claims, the level of ordinary skill, the breadth of the disclosure, and whether undue experimentation would be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity — Anticipation (prior art) for pre-AIA patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated if a single prior art reference discloses each and every limitation of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must compare the claim limitations to the prior art reference as a whole; anticipation requires that the prior art enable the claimed invention and be enabling to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity — Prior art and obviousness (post-AIA and pre-AIA distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses the applicable prior art framework for patents with effective filing dates before vs on/after March 16, 2013, and the standard for obviousness as a separate ground of invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should be instructed which statutory regime applies and, for obviousness, consider the Graham factors and relevant case law (e.g., KSR): (1) scope and content of prior art, (2) differences between prior art and claim, (3) level of ordinary skill, and (4) secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of obviousness requires identifying the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art as part of the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should consider education, experience, and technical training typical in the field when assessing what would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill at the time of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the obviousness inquiry requires evaluating what the prior art discloses relative to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should compare claim elements to the prior art, identify differences, and decide whether a person of ordinary skill would be motivated to combine references to reach the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses who is the true inventor(s) of the claimed subject matter and issues that may render a patent invalid or unenforceable when inventorship is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may be asked to resolve factual disputes about contributions to conception and whether named inventors match actual inventors under governing law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable defenses — Inequitable conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequitable conduct requires proof that the patentee acted with intent to deceive the Patent Office and withheld or misrepresented material information during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must consider materiality and intent to deceive; both are required and specific evidence must show the patentee knew of the information and intended to deceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable defenses — Laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Laches may bar equitable relief where there was an unreasonable delay in filing suit and prejudice resulted to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should consider length of delay and prejudice; follow the court's current instructions and case law on availability of laches in patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable defenses — Equitable estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable estoppel can prevent a patentee from enforcing rights if the patentee's conduct led the defendant to reasonably rely to its detriment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must assess patentee's statements or conduct, the reasonableness of the defendant's reliance, and resulting prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable defenses — Prosecution laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution laches addresses unreasonable and unexplained delay in patent prosecution that may render a patent unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury or court should evaluate the patentee's delay before the Patent Office and any resulting prejudice to the public or defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable defenses — Unclean hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Unclean hands may bar equitable relief if the patentee engaged in misconduct related to the subject matter of the lawsuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should consider whether plaintiff's misconduct is sufficiently related and serious to deny equitable remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — Introduction (compensatory standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent damages under 35 U.S.C. §284 must compensate the patent owner for the infringement and may not be less than a reasonable royalty for the use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should understand that damages aim to compensate for past infringement and may include lost profits or, alternatively, a reasonable royalty; instructions distinguish past damages from potential future royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — 'But for' test
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits damages require the patentee to show by a preponderance of the evidence that, but for the defendant's infringement, the patentee would have made additional sales and profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should apply the 'but for' causation test and evaluate showing of demand, absence/availability/acceptability of noninfringing substitutes, capacity to meet demand, and amount of profit attributable to the patented feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — Demand
rubrics_metrics.description: One element of lost profits analysis is establishing demand for the patented product during the relevant period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should consider market evidence showing customers wanted the patented features and would have purchased from the patentee but for the infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — Noninfringing substitutes — Acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: A noninfringing substitute is acceptable only if the specific purchasers of the infringing product would have accepted it as a substitute for the patented product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must assess whether buyers chose the infringing product because of patented features; acceptable substitutes must meet purchaser expectations, not merely compete in the market broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — Noninfringing substitutes — Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: A substitute is available if the defendant had the equipment, materials, know-how, and experience to design, manufacture, and sell the substitute at the time of the infringing sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should examine whether practical capability to make the substitute existed when the infringing sales occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — Capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity considers whether the patentee had the manufacturing capacity to meet the lost sales it claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should evaluate production capabilities and whether the patentee could have made the additional units 'but for' infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — Amount of profit and market share
rubrics_metrics.description: Determines the appropriate monetary measure of lost profits including the patentee's profit per unit and market share evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should calculate profits attributable to lost sales, considering gross margin, costs, and share of the market taken by the infringer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — Collateral sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers additional sales generated because of the patented product (e.g., accessory or aftermarket sales) that may be recoverable as lost profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should evaluate evidence that sales of other products were promoted by the patented product and would have been made but for the infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — Price erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures lost profits where the patentee lost the ability to charge higher prices due to the infringer's sales undercutting price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may consider how the infringer's pricing affected the patentee's pricing and profits over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Generally (entitlement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lost profits are not proven (or only partially proven), the patentee is entitled to no less than a reasonable royalty for the infringing uses it did not already recover via lost profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must determine whether the plaintiff proved a reasonable royalty amount for the portion of infringing sales not covered by lost profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Definition using the 'hypothetical negotiation' method
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the royalty that would have resulted from a hypothetical license negotiation between the patentee and the infringer just before the infringement began, assuming the patent was valid and infringed and both parties were willing to negotiate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must assume a hypothetical negotiation date and that both sides understood validity and infringement; they then estimate the royalty that a willing licensor and licensee would have agreed to under the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant factors for hypothetical negotiation (Georgia-Pacific-style factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists factors the jury may consider in determining a reasonable royalty, including (but not limited to) prior royalties, comparable patent licenses, nature/scope of the license, licensor's licensing policy, commercial relationship between parties, effect on collateral sales, patent term, product profitability and commercial success, utility/advantages of invention, nature of the commercial embodiment, extent of defendant's use, customary profit portions, portion of profit attributable to patented features vs unpatented features, expert testimony, hypothetical negotiation outcome, and any other economic factors a prudent business person would consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury may consider any of these factors as relevant evidence of the economic value of the patent; the list is non-exhaustive and the weight of each factor depends on the facts of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Multiple patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple patents are infringed, the jury may award separate royalties for each patent and consider how multiple required licenses affect the hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should account for stacking effects and the need to pay multiple royalties when multiple patents read on a single product; consider number of licenses needed and impact on negotiated royalty rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Timing (use of post-infringement evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the hypothetical negotiation date is just before infringement began, the jury may consider actual profits and commercial success after that date only if those results were foreseeable at the negotiation date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors may admit post-infringement evidence but must only consider it to the extent it would have been foreseeable just before infringement began.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Availability and cost of non-infringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: The availability and cost of acceptable noninfringing substitutes is a relevant consideration for reasonable royalty calculations; a non-infringing substitute must not include all claimed features or must be licensed under the patent to be noninfringing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must apply the same acceptability and availability inquiries used for lost profits when considering substitutes for reasonable royalty purposes; consider whether buyers purchased the product for patented features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Post-trial (future royalties for continued use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury may award a separate reasonable royalty for future use of the patented technology after the trial; this should be listed separately from past damages unless the parties would have negotiated a single royalty for the patent life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing future royalties, consider costs to switch to a noninfringing design, demand for the infringing product, use of similar technology in new products, past damages owed, and defendant's profits; jury should say whether the parties would have negotiated a single royalty covering past and future use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — Extent of defendant's use and value of that use
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor considering how much the defendant used the patented invention and any evidence showing the value derived from that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should evaluate evidence of the defendant's use and its value in assigning a royalty reflecting the benefit received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert opinion testimony for damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony of qualified economists or other specialists may be considered on the economic value of the patent and appropriate damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should weigh expert opinions alongside other evidence and consider methodology, assumptions, and relevance.
